title: serverless-prototyping-adapter-hacklab
content:
Workshop: Serverless Prototyping + Adapter Hacklab
Owner: Priya Shah (solutions-engineering)
Duration: 90 minutes recommended (45m guided + 45m hands-on)
Audience: Solutions engineers, customer devs, small platform teams wanting a fast proof-of-concept for integrating Redwood via a lightweight serverless adapter.
Goal: Ship a minimal end-to-end prototype that demonstrates routing, KV prefix caching, graceful fallback to hosted model variants, and cost-aware batching using Redwood hosted API + a serverless adapter (AWS Lambda or Vercel Function).
Why this exists (notes to self): customers repeatedly ask for a low-friction path to demo Redwood while avoiding long infra setup; serverless adapters are low ceremony and map well to PoC timelines. Keep constraints clear: not for production SLAs.

Prereqs (what attendees need):
- Redwood API key (test project)
- Node 18+ (or Deno) and npm/yarn installed locally
- AWS or Vercel account for deploying a single function (we demo Vercel because it's fastest)
- GitHub account to fork the example repo linked above

Lab outline (high-level):
1) Intro (5m): goals, architecture diagram (function -> Redwood API -> optional KV store), cost/latency expectations
2) Quick start (10m): clone repo, install, run local dev function, smoke test
3) Implement prefix/KV cache + batcher (20m): add simple in-memory LRU for local demo, wire to request flow, measure token calls saved
4) Add graceful fallback (15m): route to a cheaper model variant on quota error or latency spike; record which requests failover
5) Deploy and test (20m): deploy to Vercel or Lambda, run synthetic scenarios, capture results in a tiny local dashboard (curl + jq)
6) Debrief & next steps (10m): how to harden for Dedicated/Private, telemetry hooks to Redwood Console, POC extension ideas

Detailed steps (copy-pasta ready):
A) Clone + setup
- git clone https://github.com/redwood-inference/examples/serverless-adapter-proto.git
- cd serverless-adapter-proto
- cp .env.example .env  # fill REDWOOD_API_KEY and REDWOOD_MODEL (e.g., redwood-1-small)
- npm install
- npm run dev  # runs local function at http://localhost:3000/api/generate

B) Quick smoke test (curl)
- curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/generate -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"prompt":"Write a haiku about caching"}' | jq .
Expect: 200 + json with text output. If 401, re-check REDWOOD_API_KEY.

C) Where to add KV caching (implementation notes)
- File: src/adapter/handler.js
- Hook point: before calling Redwood API, compute a cache key = hash(model + prompt_prefix)
- Demo cache: simple in-memory Map with LRU eviction (ok for single-instance demo). For multi-instance, call out Redis or a managed KV (Dynamo, Cloudflare Workers KV)
- Pseudocode:
  const cacheKey = sha256(model + prefix(prompt, 256));
  const cached = cache.get(cacheKey);
  if (cached) return cached;
  const res = await callRedwoodAPI(payload);
  cache.set(cacheKey, res, ttlSec=3600);

D) Batching (local prototype pattern)
- For demo, implement a micro-batcher that collects requests for 20ms or until N=8 tokens/requests and then issues a single Redwood API call with multiple prompts (using Redwood's multiplex or sequential calls depending on API).
- Simple implementation: maintain an array of pending {prompt, resolve} objects and setTimeout flush at 20ms or when length >= 8.
- Note: show how batching reduces redundant model init overhead and token cost when prompts share prefixes.

E) Graceful fallback strategy
- Configurable policy: on HTTP 429/503 or latency > 2x baseline, route to a fallback model tag (e.g., redwood-1-tiny) or a cached response.
- Implementation point: wrap callRedwoodAPI in try/catch and inspect response headers: x-redwood-latency-ms, x-redwood-quota-remaining (demo header), <= use these to flip a local 'fallback' bit for 30s.
- Logging: emit events to stdout with structured JSON {event: 'fallback', reason, model_from, model_to, trace_id}.

F) Observability hints for PoC
- Add simple counters: total_requests, cache_hits, cache_misses, batch_size_histogram, fallback_count. Expose at /api/metrics (plain JSON) for quick dashboards during workshop.
- Show example curl to poll metrics and compute hit rate:
  curl http://localhost:3000/api/metrics | jq .cache_hit_rate

G) Troubleshooting (common)
- 401 errors: API key missing or scoped to different project. Check .env and REDWOOD_PROJECT_ID if used.
- Local dev cold start: if using Vercel dev, a cold serverless function may restart. Keep warm invocations (demo tip).
- Batching silent failures: unflushed promises — validate that flush is always called on shutdown and on timer intervals.

H) Sample adapter snippet (Node/Express-like pseudocode)
const pending = [];
function enqueue(prompt) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    pending.push({prompt, resolve});
    if (pending.length >= 8) flush();
    if (!flushTimer) flushTimer = setTimeout(flush, 20);
  });
}
async function flush() {
  clearTimeout(flushTimer);
  const batch = pending.splice(0, pending.length);
  const payload = {prompts: batch.map(p => p.prompt), model: currentModel};
  const res = await callRedwoodAPI(payload);
  // distribute responses
  batch.forEach((b, i) => b.resolve(res.outputs[i]));
}

I) Workshop exercise scenarios (for breakouts)
- Scenario A: Drop Redis KV and keep in-memory only. Measure how cache hit rate drops as you scale function concurrency to 5 instances.
- Scenario B: Trigger quota spike (simulate 429 responses) and observe automatic fallback to redwood-1-tiny; compute percent requests served from fallback and token-savings estimate.
- Scenario C: Introduce 50ms delay to Redwood calls and show how batching window/size should be tuned for latency vs cost tradeoff.

J) Post-workshop POC next steps checklist (customer-facing handoff)
- Replace in-memory cache with durable KV (Redis/Cloudflare/Dynamo)
- Move from serverless to Dedicated if consistent high throughput or strict SLOs are required
- Add request tracing integration (OpenTelemetry) + route traces to Redwood Console via trace hooks
- Add auth and secrets management (KMS/HSM) for PROD API keys and rotate keys regularly
- Create rollout policy in Redwood Console: canary on 5% traffic -> automatic fallback on error budget exceed

Known gaps / unresolved questions (notes):
- We currently don't have a public example of x-redwood-quota-remaining header; need to validate with runtime team whether we should rely on it for client-side fallbacks. (action: ask eng/runtime)
- Demo model names used in repo are placeholders; ensure they map to engine names available on demo project before workshop.

References & riffable snippets:
- GitHub: https://github.com/redwood-inference/examples/serverless-adapter-proto
- Internal runtime docs: CONFLUENCE-ENG-1234 (adapter guidelines)
- Example telemetry proto: https://github.com/redwood-inference/telemetry-protos

Appendix: quick checklist for facilitators
- [ ] Confirm workshop region (US-WEST recommended for lowest latency to demo project)
- [ ] Prepare 3 test accounts and API keys (isolate quota)
- [ ] Fork repo and open PR with demo changes before session start
- [ ] Have backup slides with architecture and troubleshooting notes
- [ ] Ensure attendees can access Vercel/AWS and have billing/limits allowances

End of doc.
Notes: keep this doc informal; canonicalized version should move to Confluence once we stabilize the adapter API and confirm header contract with runtime.
